newsitem.title: USA: U of Michigan preliminary May index at record.
newsitem.headline: U of Michigan preliminary May index at record.

text.p: The University of Michigan's preliminary index of consumer sentiment for May set a record high at a reading of 104.6, market sources said on Friday.
It was also the first time the index stood at a reading of 100 or higher for three consecutive months, the sources said.
"This is the highest reading ever for that index," a market source told Reuters.
The University of Michigan releases its index only to paying subscribers. Earlier on Friday, market sources said the index rose to 104.6 from 101.4 in April.
The expectations index stood at 98.6 in early May versus 92.5 in April and current conditions at 113.9 vs. 115.2.

"All these statistics can be volatile, but this number is consistent with everything else going on in the economy. We have to believe the consumer must be pretty happy with it," said Conference Board economist Michael Boldin who calculates the U.S. Leading Economic Indicators index which includes the University of Michigan's expectations index.
"You can't say it means a lot more to have a reading at 104.6 rather than at 101, but it really means the consumer is very confident," Boldin added.
A market source also said "it's the first time the index is at 100 or more for three months in a row, 104.6, 101.4 in April, 100 in March."
The only other instance when the University of Michigan's index read in the three digits in the same year, though not in consecutive months, was in 1984, the source also said.

"We can't say this is the best the economy has ever been but certainly that it's is doing well, especially for the consumer. There no disagreement out there, no belief the consumer will be a drag in the economy," Boldin said.
Boldin also said the buoyant confidence among Americans bodes well for future growth since two-thirds of the U.S. economy is fueled by consumer spending.
"The consumer may not spend enough to keep the economy growing at 5.0 percent, but certainly enough to generate nothing less than trend growth or a little more," he added.

Boldin declined to read too much into the fresh rise in the expectations component except that "the consumer seems to be telling us these good times will continue into the future" -- a trend confirmed by The Conference Board's own index of consumer confidence.

David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International, said the record reading "is a clear demonstration that, in an environment of healthy growth, low inflation and low unemployment, the consumer is very upbeat."

Commenting on the similar levels of high consumer confidence in 1984 and 1997, Resler made the point that Americans were relieved 13 years ago about a high rate of inflation being brought down and a deep recession being over.
"This time, it's because everything has been going so well for so long and the consumer feels it's likely to continue," Resler added.
